narrative:
The model determined that you have a 90% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

Three factors weighed most heavily in this decision. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the single biggest reason the model expected you to struggle. Being in the bottom decile—far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 19.3 was the second most important factor; it sits well below the 37-point average of students who were admitted and pulled the outlook even further in the negative direction. Finally, your first-year class ranking in the lowest decile (compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants) added more weight toward the same conclusion.

None of these academic signals suggested you were on track to pass the bar. Although your family income, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played no role in the decision, the model saw your early and continued low performance as clear indicators of future difficulty.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, then focus on raising your grades dramatically in any additional coursework. Once you have concrete evidence of stronger academic performance, reapply. Many students improve these exact areas and go on to succeed.
